questions.q: What is the position of the Moon during a solar eclipse?
questions.a: During a solar eclipse, the Moon is positioned between the Earth and the Sun. A student who says "the Sun is between the Earth and Moon" confuses the alignment and fails to realize that the Moon is the one casting the shadow on Earth.

questions.q: Why does the Moon disappear or turn dark during a lunar eclipse?
questions.a: The Moon turns dark because the Earth blocks sunlight from reaching the Moon's surface. If a student thinks the Moon itself "runs out of light," they miss the concept of the Earth acting as an opaque barrier that casts a shadow into space.

questions.q: If you are standing in a location experiencing a solar eclipse, what do you see when you look at the Sun?
questions.a: You see the Moon blocking part or all of the Sun's light. First, identify the order: Sun -> Moon -> Earth. Since the Moon is between you and the Sun, it acts as a screen. A wrong answer suggests the student doesn't understand that the Moon is opaque and physically obstructs our line of sight to the Sun.

questions.q: Compare the shadow-casting object in a solar eclipse versus a lunar eclipse.
questions.a: In a solar eclipse, the Moon casts the shadow; in a lunar eclipse, the Earth casts the shadow. If a student says the Sun casts the shadow, they have fundamentally misunderstood that the Sun is the light *source*, not the object being shadowed.

questions.q: Is it possible for a solar eclipse to happen at night? Justify your answer.
questions.a: No, because a solar eclipse requires the Sun to be visible in the sky to be blocked by the Moon. If a student answers "yes," they are ignoring the fact that the Sun is on the opposite side of the Earth at night.

questions.q: Imagine you have a torch (Sun), a small ball (Moon), and a globe (Earth). How would you arrange them to show a lunar eclipse?
questions.a: The order must be Torch -> Globe -> Ball. The student must demonstrate that the Earth (globe) is in the middle, intercepting the light from the torch. A poor answer would place the ball in the middle, which would represent a solar eclipse.
